questions.problem:
Given that 

$$
h(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}-{k}^{2}}{x-k}, & x\ne k \\ -4, & x=k\end{aligned}
$$

is continuous at $x=k$, find the value of the constant $k.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we factor the numerator and cancel any common factors: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}-{k}^{2}}{x-k} & =\frac{(x+k)(x-k)}{(x-k)} \\  & =\frac{(x+k)\cancel{(x-k)}}{\cancel{x-k}} \\  & =x+k\end{aligned}
$$

We then can compute the limit at $x=k,$ and we get

$$
{lim}_{x\to k}h(x)={lim}_{x\to k}(x+k)=k+k=2k.
$$

For $h(x)$ to be continuous at $x=k,$ we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}h(k) & ={lim}_{x\to k}h(x) \\ -4 & =2k \\ k & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, for the function to be continuous at $x=k,$ we need $k=-2.$

Let $g(x)$ be the function defined below. For what values of $k$ is $g(x)$ continuous at $x=2?$

$$
g(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}-4}{{x}^{2}-6x+8}, & x\ne 2 \\ {k}^{2}-3k-12, & x=2\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we factor the numerator and denominator and cancel any common factors:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}-4}{{x}^{2}-6x+8} & =\frac{(x+2)(x-2)}{(x-4)(x-2)} \\  & =\frac{(x+2)\cancel{(x-2)}}{(x-4)\cancel{(x-2)}} \\  & =\frac{x+2}{x-4}\end{aligned}
$$

We then can compute the limit at $x=2,$ and we get

$$
{lim}_{x\to 2}g(x)={lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{x+2}{x-4}=\frac{2+2}{2-4}=-2.
$$

For $g(x)$ to be continuous at $x=2,$ we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}g(2) & ={lim}_{x\to 2}g(x) \\ {k}^{2}-3k-12 & =-2 \\ {k}^{2}-3k-10 & =0 \\ (k+2)(k-5) & =0 \\ k & =-2,\,5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, for the function to be continuous at $x=2,$ we need $k=-2$ or $k=5.$

Let $g(x)$ be the function defined below. For what value of $k$ is $g(x)$ continuous at $x=1?$

$$
g(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}+2x-3}{kx-k}, & x\ne 1 \\ k, & x=1\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we factor the numerator and denominator and cancel any common factors:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}+2x-3}{kx-k} & =\frac{(x+3)(x-1)}{k(x-1)} \\  & =\frac{(x+3)\cancel{(x-1)}}{k\cancel{(x-1)}} \\  & =\frac{x+3}{k}\end{aligned}
$$

We then can compute the limit at $x=1,$ and we get

$$
{lim}_{x\to 1}g(x)={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{x+3}{k}=\frac{4}{k}.
$$

For $g(x)$ to be continuous at $x=1,$ we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}g(1) & ={lim}_{x\to 1}g(x) \\ k & =\frac{4}{k} \\ {k}^{2} & =4 \\ k & =\pm 2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, for the function to be continuous at $x=1,$ we need $k=\pm 2.$

Let $f(x)$ be the function defined below. Find the value of $a,$ if any, for which $f(x)$ is continuous at $x=2.$

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{x-2}, & x<2 \\ ax, & x\ge 2\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
From the definition of $f(x),$ the left-sided limit of $f(x)$ at $x=2$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {2}^{-}}f(x)={lim}_{x\to {2}^{-}}\frac{1}{x-2}=-\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

On the other hand, the right-sided limit is

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {2}^{+}}f(x)={lim}_{x\to {2}^{+}}ax=2a.\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${lim}_{x\to 2}f(x)=-\infty ,$ there is no value of $a$ that makes $f(x)$ continuous at $x=2.$

questions.problem:
Let $g(x)$ be the function defined below. For what values of $k$ is $g(x)$ continuous at $x=-3?$

$$
g(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}+14x+33}{2kx+6k}, & x<-3 \\ -\frac{kx}{3}, & x\ge -3\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
From the definition of $g(x)$, the left-sided limit of $g(x)$ at $x=-3$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -{3}^{-}}g(x) & ={lim}_{x\to -{3}^{-}}\frac{{x}^{2}+14x+33}{2kx+6k} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to -{3}^{-}}\frac{(x+11)(x+3)}{2k(x+3)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to -{3}^{-}}\frac{(x+11)\cancel{(x+3)}}{2k\cancel{(x+3)}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to -{3}^{-}}\frac{x+11}{2k} \\  & =\frac{4}{k}.\end{aligned}
$$

On the other hand, the right-sided limit is

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -{3}^{+}}g(x) & ={lim}_{x\to -{3}^{+}}(-\frac{kx}{3}) \\  & =-\frac{k(-3)}{3} \\  & =k.\end{aligned}
$$

We also note that $g(-3)=k.$ 

So, for $g(x)$ to be continuous at $x=-3,$ we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -{3}^{+}}g(x) & ={lim}_{x\to -{3}^{-}}g(x) \\ k & =\frac{4}{k} \\ {k}^{2} & =4 \\ k & =\pm 2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $k=-2$ or $k=2$ remove the discontinuity at $x=-3.$

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we factor the numerator and denominator and cancel any common factors:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{3}+1}{kx+k} & =\frac{(x+1)({x}^{2}-x+1)}{k(x+1)} \\  & =\frac{\cancel{(x+1)}({x}^{2}-x+1)}{k\cancel{(x+1)}} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}-x+1}{k}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now we can compute the limit at $x=-1,$ and get

$$
\lim_\limits{x\to -1} g(x) = \lim_\limits{x\to -1} \left(\dfrac{x^2-x+1}{k}\right) = \dfrac{3}{k}.
$$

For $g(x)$ to be continuous at $x=-1,$ we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -1}g(x) & =g(-1) \\ \frac{3}{k} & =\frac{k}{3} \\ 9 & ={k}^{2} \\ \pm 3 & =k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, for the function to be continuous at $x=-1,$ the value of $k$ must be either $-3$ or $3.$

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
From the definition of $f(x)$, the left-sided limit of $f(x)$ at $x=2$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {2}^{-}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {2}^{-}}\frac{{x}^{2}+4x-12}{{x}^{2}-4} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {2}^{-}}\frac{(x-2)(x+6)}{(x-2)(x+2)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {2}^{-}}\frac{\cancel{(x-2)}(x+6)}{\cancel{(x-2)}(x+2)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {2}^{-}}\frac{x+6}{x+2} \\  & =\frac{2+6}{2+2} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

On the other hand, the right-sided limit is

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {2}^{+}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {2}^{+}}{2}^{kx} \\  & ={2}^{2k}.\end{aligned}
$$

We also note that $f(2) = 2^{2k}.$

So, for $f(x)$ to be continuous at $x=2,$ we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {2}^{+}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {2}^{-}}f(x) \\ {2}^{2k} & =2 \\ {2}^{2k} & ={2}^{1} \\ 2k & =1 \\ k & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $k=\dfrac12$ removes the discontinuity at $x=2.$

tutorials.problem:
Consider the function $f(x)$ below:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14196844/assets/cbdbe44a94ff036c74957691e30ed3652d50d2a8dbaa50b29827408f242492bb.svg)

The function $f(x)$ seems to have a point discontinuity at $x=1.$ However, by selecting a particular value for $k,$ we can remove the point discontinuity and make the function continuous.

We can find this value of $k$ by forcing the limit of the function to be equal to the value of the function at $x=1\mathbin{:}$

$$
\lim\limits_{x\to 1} f(x) = f(1)
$$

Remember that $\lim\limits_{x\to 1} f(x)$ represents the value that $f(x)$ approaches as $x$ gets closer and closer, but not equal, to $1.$ So, when evaluating $\lim\limits_{x\to 1} f(x),$ we need to use the function definition for $x \neq 1.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 1}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{{x}^{2}-1}{{x}^{2}+x-2} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{(x-1)(x+1)}{(x-1)(x+2)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{\cancel{(x-1)}(x+1)}{\cancel{(x-1)}(x+2)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{x+1}{x+2} \\  & =\frac{1+1}{1+2} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

At $x=1,$ the function is defined as $f(x)=k.$ So, $f(1)=k$, and for continuity we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 1}f(x) & =f(1) \\ \frac{2}{3} & =k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, to make $f(x)$ continuous at $x=1,$ we need to choose $k=\dfrac{2}{3}.$

tutorials.title: Introduction
tutorials.content:
Consider the function $f(x)$ below:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14196844/assets/cbdbe44a94ff036c74957691e30ed3652d50d2a8dbaa50b29827408f242492bb.svg)

The function $f(x)$ seems to have a point discontinuity at $x=1.$ However, by selecting a particular value for $k,$ we can remove the point discontinuity and make the function continuous.

We can find this value of $k$ by forcing the limit of the function to be equal to the value of the function at $x=1\mathbin{:}$

$$
\lim\limits_{x\to 1} f(x) = f(1)
$$

Remember that $\lim\limits_{x\to 1} f(x)$ represents the value that $f(x)$ approaches as $x$ gets closer and closer, but not equal, to $1.$ So, when evaluating $\lim\limits_{x\to 1} f(x),$ we need to use the function definition for $x \neq 1.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 1}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{{x}^{2}-1}{{x}^{2}+x-2} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{(x-1)(x+1)}{(x-1)(x+2)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{\cancel{(x-1)}(x+1)}{\cancel{(x-1)}(x+2)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{x+1}{x+2} \\  & =\frac{1+1}{1+2} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

At $x=1,$ the function is defined as $f(x)=k.$ So, $f(1)=k$, and for continuity we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 1}f(x) & =f(1) \\ \frac{2}{3} & =k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, to make $f(x)$ continuous at $x=1,$ we need to choose $k=\dfrac{2}{3}.$
